details.readme:
![claude-bughunter banner](assets/banner-v2.svg) # claude-bughunter > A self-contained Claude skill bundle for bug hunting and external red-team work · **83 skills** · 15 slash commands · **681 disclosed-report patterns** (433 now individually cited & auditable) across 24 core vulnerability classes · enterprise identity + infrastructure attack matrices · engagement-folder scaffolding · Burp MCP integration · battle-tested across authorized red-team and bug-hunting engagements, plus public training platforms (DVWA, OWASP Juice Shop, Hacker101, testphp.vulnweb.com). Built by **[Sachin Sharma](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sachinsharma8080/)** — Bug Hunting & GenAI Security Research.

SPONSORED BY
    

--- ## What is this? `claude-bughunter` is a drop-in skill bundle for the [Claude Code skills system](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/skills). Install once and Claude Code stops being a chatbot and starts behaving like a senior bug-hunting researcher or red-team operator: it knows the techniques, the chain templates, the VRT mappings, the platform CVE chains, and the hygiene — and it stays in scope. Four layers stack: - **Think** — `bb-methodology` + `redteam-mindset`: the 5-phase non-linear workflow, critical-thinking framework, and red-team operator discipline. - **Hunt webapps** — 58 `hunt-*` skills curated from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports: per-class detection patterns, payloads, bypass tables, and chain templates. - **Hit the perimeter** — enterprise platform chains (M365/Entra, Okta, vCenter, SSL-VPN appliances, SharePoint, cloud IAM): current 2024–2026 CVE chains + post-credential escalation. - **Ship it** — `triage-validation` + reporting + `evidence-hygiene`: the 7-Question Gate, VRT-aware severity, OOS rebuttals, PII redaction, and red-team deliverables. All triggered automatically by topic — describe what you're testing in plain English and the relevant skill loads. No invocation by name. --- ## Quickstart **Option A — install as a Claude Code plugin (recommended).** From inside Claude Code: ```text /plugin marketplace add elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter /plugin install claude-bughunter@elementalsouls ``` All 83 skills + 15 commands load namespaced under `claude-bughunter:` and update when you bump the plugin version — no files copied into `~/.claude/`. **A HackerOne account is optional.** The install asks for a HackerOne API username and token. They only let the HackerOne MCP read your private programs and your own reports; leave both blank if you don't need that. Every skill, command and the MCP's public tools (duplicate search, program scope) work without them. **Option B — copy install (no plugin system / pin to a clone):** ```bash git clone https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter.git cd Claude-BugHunter ``` ```bash # macOS / Linux bash scripts/install.sh # Windows (PowerShell) pwsh ./scripts/install.ps1 ``` Both copy the skills + commands into `~/.claude/` (macOS/Linux) or `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\` (Windows) and wire the `hunt` engagement scaffolder. **What each install path gives you:** | Path | 83 skills + 15 slash commands | `cbh` CLI | `hunt` scaffolder | |---|---|---|---| | **A — plugin** | ✅ namespaced under `claude-bughunter:` | ➕ separate `pipx install` | ❌ clone-only | | **B — copy install** | ✅ copied into `~/.claude/` | ✅ from the clone | ✅ from the clone | The plugin is the fastest path to the skills + slash commands. The terminal-native `cbh` runner installs standalone — `pipx install git+https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter` — so plugin users can add it without a full clone (see [`cbh` CLI](docs/cbh-cli.md)). The `hunt` engagement scaffolder ships with the clone (Option B). That's it. Open Claude Code and describe what you're testing in plain English — the right skill loads automatically, no invocation by name: ```text > Testing acme.com — an in-scope HackerOne target. Run recon and rank the surface. ⟳ loading skills: web2-recon, offensive-osint, bb-methodology … → subdomain enum (subfinder + crt.sh) … 47 hosts → live hosts (httpx) … 12 · tech fingerprint … 6 distinct stacks → ranked surface: api.acme.com (GraphQL, introspection ON) ← start here auth.acme.com (OAuth, SSO) ← hunt-oauth Next: want me to probe the GraphQL introspection + OAuth redirect_uri? ``` → Full [Installation guide](INSTALL.md) · [Usage guide](USAGE.md) · [searchable skill catalog](docs/skills.md). > The block above is an illustrative transcript. To record a real demo of your own session: `asciinema rec demo.cast` → upload to [asciinema.org](https://asciinema.org) and drop the badge here. --- ## Runs on multiple agent harnesses ![One install, agent harnesses — Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex CLI, Hermes Agent, Google AntiGravity](assets/harness-routing.svg) The skills are plain [Agent Skills](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/skills) — the same `SKILL.md` format that **Claude Code · OpenCode · OpenAI Codex CLI · Hermes Agent · Google AntiGravity** all load. One command installs them everywhere: ```bash # macOS / Linux bash scripts/install.sh --all --burp-mcp # Windows (PowerShell) pwsh ./scripts/install.ps1 -All -BurpMcp ``` | Harness | Target Skill Directory | Flag | |---|---|---| | **Claude Code** (baseline) | `~/.claude/skills/` | *(default)* | | **OpenCode** | reads `~/.claude/skills/` & `~/.agents/skills/` | *(default)* / `--agents` | | **OpenAI Codex CLI** | `~/.agents/skills/` | `--agents` | | **Hermes Agent** | `~/.hermes/skills/` | `--hermes` | | **Google AntiGravity** | `~/.gemini/config/skills/` | `--antigravity` | `--all` (`-All`) detects installed harnesses and copies skills to each harness's path (`~/.claude/skills`, `~/.agents/skills`, `~/.hermes/skills`, `~/.gemini/config/skills`); `--burp-mcp` (`-BurpMcp`) wires the Burp MCP server into each. The full *knowledge* layer ports to all five — the slash commands and `/hunt` engine stay Claude-Code-only by design. → [Multi-harness guide](docs/multi-harness.md) --- ## Star History Chart is self-hosted — regenerate with `python3 scripts/gen_star_history.py` (needs `gh auth login`). Refreshes automatically each day via `.github/workflows/star-history.yml`. --- ## Scope — what this bundle is for, and what it isn't This bundle covers the **external attack surface** — anything reachable from the internet without first compromising an internal endpoint. ### In scope - **Bug bounty hunting** — web apps, APIs, SaaS, GraphQL, OAuth, JWT, file upload, IDOR, SSRF, RCE chains - **Web application pentesting** — full hunt-* coverage of OWASP-mapped bug classes + discipline rules - **External red-team engagements** — initial-access against internet-facing enterprise estate: M365 / Entra ID, Okta-as-IdP, SharePoint on-prem (ToolShell + legacy SOAP), VMware vCenter / Workspace ONE, SSL VPN appliances (Cisco / Fortinet / Citrix / Palo Alto / Pulse / SonicWall / F5), Android APK red-team, supply-chain recon - **Cloud misconfig + post-credential escalation** — public S3, IMDS chains, STS AssumeRole, cross-account confused-deputy - **Recon + OSINT** — subdomain enum, identity-fabric mapping, certificate transparency, JS analysis, secret scanning - **Reporting** — H1, Bugcrowd (VRT-aware), Intigriti, Immunefi, plus client-facing red-team deliverable format ### Out of scope (deliberate — not gaps, design decisions) - **Internal Active Directory attacks** — BloodHound, Kerberoasting, ASREProast, DCSync, Pass-the-Hash, AD CS abuse, ntlmrelayx, Responder, PetitPotam, etc. Different operational risk profile; needs different tooling and judgment. **Future bundle, not this one.** - **C2 frameworks** — Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Mythic, Havoc, BRC4 tradecraft. Out of scope for external-only engagement model. - **Post-exploit / persistence / lateral** — Mimikatz/comsvcs LSASS dumping, golden/silver tickets, named-pipe impersonation, persistence (registry, scheduled tasks, WMI events, COM hijacking), token theft. These start after the perimeter has already broken — different bundle territory. - **Evasion** — AMSI bypass, ETW patching, AV/EDR bypass. Tied to C2 tradecraft above. - **iOS pentesting / hardware / RF / ICS** — out of scope by design. - **Binary exploitation / kernel pwn / browser internals** — different skill universe. If you're running an internal red team that includes domain-takeover chains via Kerberos or lateral movement, **this bundle won't help you in those phases** — and we'd rather say that up front than have you find out mid-engagement. The external surface handoff to internal-RT tooling (Impacket, NetExec, CrackMapExec, Rubeus, Certify, BloodHound) is intentionally outside our scope. **Coverage for internal AD and post-exploit may come in a future update.** --- ## What's inside **83 skills**, auto-loaded by topic — no invocation by name. Coverage across the external attack surface: | Category | # | Examples | |---|---|---| | Hunt — web app vuln classes | 58 | XSS, SQLi, SSRF, IDOR, LFI, SSTI, XXE, CSRF, CORS, open-redirect, SharePoint, ASP.NET/NTLM | | Enterprise platform attack ★ | 10 | M365/Entra, Okta, cloud-IAM-deep, vCenter, enterprise VPN, APK/iOS red-team pipelines, supply-chain recon | | Reporting & validation | 6 | triage-validation, evidence-hygiene, report-writing, bugcrowd-reporting | | Recon & OSINT | 5 | web2-recon, offensive-osint, osint-methodology, recon-scope-triage | | Methodology & mindset | 4 | bb-methodology, bug-bounty, redteam-mindset, bb-local-toolkit | Full searchable catalog → **[docs/skills.md](docs/skills.md)**. Also ships **15 slash commands** (`/hunt`, `/recon`, `/report`, …) and a deterministic **engagement engine** (`engine/`) that maps a target's attack surface and routes each finding to the skill that handles it. --- ## How it works A 6-phase, non-linear workflow — **recon → map & rank → hunt → validate → report** — with scope enforced in code and a **7-Question Gate** before anything is submitted. Two ways to drive it: - **Plain English** — describe what you're testing and the relevant skill loads automatically. - **`/hunt` scaffold + `cbh` CLI** — engagement-folder structure, state, and orchestration. → [Usage guide & worked example](USAGE.md) · [6-phase architecture & skill-to-phase map](docs/architecture.md) · [`cbh` CLI](docs/cbh-cli.md) --- ## Authorization These skills are intended for assets you **own** or have **written authorization to assess** (bug-bounty in-scope assets, pentest engagement letters, CTF challenges, your own infrastructure). The skills include validation gates that auto-trigger when you point Claude at unverified third-party targets — `triage-validation`'s 7-Question Gate explicitly asks whether the asset is in scope (Q3) and on the program's accepted-impact list (Q2). # OpenRig

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@openrig/cli)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@openrig/cli) [![npm downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dw/@openrig/cli)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@openrig/cli) [![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/github/license/mvschwarz/openrig)](LICENSE) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/mvschwarz/openrig?style=social)](https://github.com/mvschwarz/openrig/stargazers)

A harness wraps a model. A rig wraps your harnesses. Define your agent team in YAML, boot it with one command. Claude Code and Codex in the same rig, managed as one system.

OpenRig is open-source software for building and running your own network of agents. It turns AI coding agents from a pile of terminal sessions into a persistent, organized team. Talk to a lead agent about the outcome you want; it can coordinate specialists across teams and bring you results and decisions that need your attention. Start with a repository and one useful change, then keep the team's work and context at the same addresses.

It's the open-source system behind my AI civilization experiments.

**Guide:** [Getting started](docs/reference/quickstart.md) · **Stuck?** [Help](docs/reference/help.md) · **Questions:** [Q&A](https://github.com/mvschwarz/openrig/discussions/92) · **Updates and demos:** [@_feralmachine on X](https://x.com/_feralmachine)

## See it running

![The OpenRig TUI: the build rig as a graph, then as a table of seats with runtime, model, context and state, then one seat in detail (real recording, 10 seconds)](assets/readme/openrig-agents-working.gif)

**Start here:** [the guided first-use path](docs/reference/quickstart.md): install, talk to OpenRig's operator, then choose a team for your first useful change.

Not setting this up today? Get the next walkthrough and occasional OpenRig updates → https://openrig.dev/follow

## Install and first run

**Let your coding agent set it up.** First check that `node --version` shows 22 or 24: the command below needs
Node.js and the `npx` that comes with it. Then, in your project folder, add OpenRig's `rigs` skill to the agent you
use:

```sh
# Claude Code
npx skills add https://github.com/mvschwarz/openrig/tree/v0.7.20/skills/rigs --skill rigs --agent claude-code
# Codex
npx skills add https://github.com/mvschwarz/openrig/tree/v0.7.20/skills/rigs --skill rigs --agent codex
# OMP (Oh My Pi): the pi target installs to .agents/skills, which OMP reads
npx skills add https://github.com/mvschwarz/openrig/tree/v0.7.20/skills/rigs --skill rigs --agent pi
```

**OMP:** this pin installs the shared skill only. The `v0.7.20` skill does not yet include OMP attachment guidance,
and complete setup from OMP has not been verified. OMP isn't a kernel provider; Claude Code or Codex must still be
signed in.

Then type `/rigs` in Claude Code, `$rigs` in Codex, or `/skill:rigs` in OMP (after `/reload-plugins` if OMP was already
open), and say what you want built. The skill has your agent tell you what it will run and change before it does,
install OpenRig, open the OpenRig view and pass your goal to OpenRig's operator. If Claude Code was already running
when you added the skill, type `/reload-skills` first, or start
a new session: a session doesn't see a skills folder created after it started.

You need Node.js 22 or 24 (22 on Apple silicon), tmux, macOS or Linux (WSL2 on Windows), and Claude Code or Codex
signed in. One provider is enough to start.

Already have OpenRig? Use the tag that matches `rig --version`, or upgrade first.

Prefer to type the commands yourself? [Install it yourself ↓](#install-it-yourself)

Setting up Node.js on Linux, on a Mac where you aren't an administrator, or on Windows (WSL2)? See [Before you start](docs/reference/getting-started.md#before-you-start).

> **What OpenRig changes on your machine**
> - **Install:** `@openrig/cli` goes in globally with npm.
> - **Setup:** `rig setup` adds an OpenRig block to `~/.tmux.conf`. It can install tmux (with Homebrew on macOS), and
>   Herdr unless you pass `--no-herdr`. Plain `rig setup`, which is what the one-command install runs, checks both
>   Claude Code and Codex and may install a missing one; `rig setup --providers claude` (or `codex`) limits it to
>   yours.
> - **Starting OpenRig, for the coding agent you use** (paths are the usual defaults):
>   - Codex: hooks and trust in `~/.codex/config.toml`.
>   - Claude Code: workspace trust in `~/.claude.json`, and activity hooks in the project's
>     `.claude/settings.local.json`, plus a status line unless you already have your own.
>   - Discovery skills go in `~/.claude/skills` and `~/.agents/skills`.
> - **Starting a team in your project:** adds managed guidance to `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`, plus the team's skills
>   and plugins.
> - **Permissions:** by default, OpenRig's own kernel gets broader permissions than a project team gets by default.
>   On Codex that's full access with no approval prompts (`-s danger-full-access -a never`). On Claude Code, its file
>   tools, web fetches and operational commands, including reads under your home folder, run without asking. A
>   permission policy, per-agent choice or Codex profile changes that. What your team can do depends on the team you
>   choose and your settings; `workshop`, for example, ships with broad access.
> - **Backups:** OpenRig doesn't guarantee it can preserve or roll back these files, so back them up first.
>
> [Everything OpenRig writes, and why →](https://github.com/mvschwarz/openrig#what-openrig-changes-on-your-machine)

### Install it yourself

This runs OpenRig's install script from the `v0.7.20` release. It checks Node.js and npm, installs the latest published `@openrig/cli` with `npm install -g`, runs the Node.js and SQLite check, then runs `rig setup --dry-run` and `rig setup`. The first line prints that plan and changes nothing:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mvschwarz/openrig/v0.7.20/scripts/install.sh | sh -s -- --dry-run
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mvschwarz/openrig/v0.7.20/scripts/install.sh | sh
```

If the last step isn't ready, the installer reports `INSTALLED, SETUP NOT COMPLETE` and points to the details from `rig setup` above. Follow that output and any reported Fix, then rerun `rig setup`; the CLI does not need reinstalling. If the only remaining failures are provider sign-ins, sign in to each selected provider as below and continue.

**Or step by step:**

```bash
npm install -g @openrig/cli
rig setup --dry-run
```

To install with Bun instead, run `bun add -g @openrig/cli`. OpenRig still runs on Node.js, so install Node.js 22 as well. Bun may block this package's postinstall script, in which case the Node.js and SQLite check described under [what OpenRig changes on your machine](#what-openrig-changes-on-your-machine) does not run at install time.

npm 11 and later can skip that postinstall script and print `npm warn install-scripts` naming `@openrig/cli`. That's expected: the CLI still works, and only the Node.js and SQLite check was skipped. To run it yourself, use `node "$(npm root -g)/@openrig/cli/scripts/check-abi.mjs"`; `rig doctor` checks the Node.js version only.

Choose the working account you already have: **Claude Code, Codex, or both**. Reuse an explicit choice; no second subscription is required. `rig setup --dry-run` previews the broader setup; applying `rig setup` checks both harnesses and installs a missing one, plus Herdr unless declined with `--no-herdr`. Pass the choice with `--providers claude` or `--providers codex` so the other reads not selected instead of failed. The one-command install above doesn't know the choice, so it installs and checks both; for one provider, go step by step and run `rig setup --providers <choice>`. On macOS, the installing agent offers Ghostty once. Setup leaves an existing cmux installation alone. It is optional for the [selected-provider path](docs/reference/getting-started.md#choose-your-providers).

A team seat with no permission policy, per-seat choice or (for Codex) named profile launches with OpenRig's [team default](docs/reference/rig-spec.md#team-launch-defaults): Claude runs ordinary `rig` commands, project reads and common tests without prompting, while lifecycle commands such as `rig up` and `rig down` still ask; Codex also gets the OpenRig workspace and its pod's state directory as writable directories. Before launching, your agent recommends keeping that default, and offers to remember selected OpenRig commands in your native settings only if you want that, at personal project scope unless you explicitly choose user-wide sessions. It is not global YOLO or permission to invent work. On Yes, the agent [adds and verifies native rules](docs/reference/getting-started.md#have-your-agent-configure-permissions); No or no answer keeps the team default and leaves settings unchanged. An existing explicit choice is reused. Say “Undo the OpenRig command allowances added by this setup” to remove only its additions.

If permission prompts are slowing you down, consider the
[workshop bundle](https://openrig.dev/rigs/workshop). It ships with broad access
and [non-interruptive mode](docs/reference/non-interruptive-mode.md): its agents
bypass permission prompts and supported harness warning dialogs. The listing
and before-install view explain that access before you choose it.

Check `tmux -V` and only your selected CLI/login: `claude --version` plus
`claude auth status`, or `codex --version` plus `codex login status`. If needed,
sign in once with `claude auth login` or `codex login`; do not install or log in
to an unused provider.

### Your agent opens OpenRig for you

After installing, your agent opens the OpenRig TUI and the operator for you. To get back to them later, ask your
agent for OpenRig or your agents in any words. After checking the selected login, it starts the daemon if it's stopped
and opens the view:

```sh
rig daemon start
rig terminal open saved:kernel --window
```

`--window` opens a new terminal tab or window itself, or a space in your current
Herdr session. Below 120 measured columns,
the **operator** fills the first page; from 120, the dashboard and operator share
it equally. The advisor has a separate tab or tmux window.
An installing agent can run it from its shell on the daemon's
desktop; the person copies nothing. It uses Herdr when installed, otherwise
the same layout in plain tmux, and preserves existing conversations. `rig tui`
is the team dashboard. Installation is finished when you are talking to the
operator; if you choose to talk later, that handoff remains pending.

If setup stops, read the named step: missing tools and selected-provider logins
need their specific setup action. A harness permission rule, sandbox or automatic
permission decision can also block the installing agent's command. The agent
should name the command and reported reason, then help you resolve that specific
step within your chosen permissions. A permission refusal is not an OpenRig
installation result.

The desktop may need an Automation approval; SSH/headless sessions may have no
display. Herdr can show first-run panels, and an 80×24 window can cramp the view.
Follow [the OpenRig view checks and next steps](docs/reference/getting-started.md#what-can-interrupt-installation-and-the-openrig-view).
Herdr is visible only inside a terminal you can see. Changing the shared TUI to
`:terminals` does not open that terminal. The agent checks the visible window when
it has desktop access and says what it could not verify otherwise. Over headless
SSH, it asks you to open a new terminal window or tab and gives the exact connection
and attachment command for the current view. If you choose a manual attachment
after a failure,
ask the installing agent for the exact command using your current operator
session; run that in a new terminal window.

# Mirli **The free, open-source, local alternative to ElevenLabs and Suno.** Sound effects, music, songs with lyrics, speech and voice cloning from open-weight models on your own GPU. Arrange it on a timeline, or let Claude Code, Cursor or any MCP agent do it. No account, no credits, works offline. MIT. Mirli was formerly Soundbox. The repository, the `soundbox` command, the `soundbox.*` MCP tools and the installer file names keep the old name for now. Environment variables are `MIRLI_*`, and the old `SOUNDBOX_*` names still work (0.5.0 and earlier read only `SOUNDBOX_*`). [Download](#download) · [Hear it](#hear-it) · [For agents](#for-agents) · [Models](#models) · [Docs](#docs) · [Website](https://mirli.app/) · [Patreon](https://patreon.com/soundboxai) [![Latest release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/HamSanders/soundbox?label=release)](https://github.com/HamSanders/soundbox/releases/latest) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/github/downloads/HamSanders/soundbox/total?label=downloads)](https://github.com/HamSanders/soundbox/releases) [![MIT licence](https://img.shields.io/badge/licence-MIT-2ea44f)](LICENSE) [![MCP server](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-24%20tools-6b4fbb)](docs/MCP.md) [![Patreon](https://img.shields.io/badge/Patreon-support-f96854?logo=patreon&logoColor=white)](https://patreon.com/soundboxai) **Watch:** [30-second tour](https://mirli.app/media/soundbox-vibe.mp4) · [Under the hood](https://mirli.app/media/soundbox-tech.mp4) · [Agents and MCP](https://mirli.app/media/soundbox-agents.mp4)
## Describe it, hear it, arrange it | Make | Arrange | Connect | |---|---|---| | Sound effects and ambience from a description | A multi-track timeline with effects, MIDI and mixdown | An MCP server with 24 tools for Claude Code and Cursor | | Instrumentals, or songs from a lyric sheet | Cast saved voices onto the lines of a script | A local HTTP API on port 17494 | | Speech, voice cloning and voice conversion | Extend, cover, repaint, split into stems | Three agent skills, including a full sound pass | Four models are verified end to end and on by default; 61 more can be switched on from the Models page. Each model's licence is shown before you download it. Everything stays in one SQLite file and a folder of WAVs under `~/.mirli`. Profiles give you several libraries in one install, one per game or client, switched from the header without a restart; the models are shared.
More screenshots · library, create, details, voices
| | | |---|---| | | | | **Library.** Every take in one list, with the player along the bottom. | **Create.** Music, SFX and Speech tabs beside the track list. | | | | | **Details.** Waveform, edits and the exact settings that made it. | **Voice Lab.** Your voices, and a side-by-side compare. | | | | | **New voice.** Clone it, pick a built-in, or import one. | **Clone.** Up to five clips of one speaker, recorded or uploaded. |
## Download The [download page](https://mirli.app/download/) picks the installer for your system. Or take one directly: | Platform | Installer | |---|---| | **Windows** 10 and 11 (x64) | [`Soundbox_x.y.z_x64-setup.exe`](https://mirli.app/download/) | | **macOS**, Apple silicon | [`Soundbox_x.y.z_aarch64.dmg`](https://mirli.app/download/) | | **macOS**, Intel | [`Soundbox_x.y.z_x64.dmg`](https://mirli.app/download/) | | **Linux** x64 (glibc 2.35+) | [`Soundbox_x.y.z_amd64.AppImage` or `.deb`](https://github.com/HamSanders/soundbox/releases/latest) | The installer carries its own runtime. The builds are not signed yet, so the first launch asks you to confirm ([where](docs/DESKTOP.md#installing)). Open SFX, describe the material, the action and the space, and generate: the first model downloads when you pick it, with its licence shown first. | Hardware | What to expect | |---|---| | NVIDIA GPU (Windows, Linux) | CUDA. A few GB of VRAM covers the verified models; MiniMax Music 3 wants about 10 GB. | | AMD or Intel GPU | Runs on the CPU unless you set `MIRLI_AUDIOCPP_BACKEND=vulkan` ([how](docs/AUDIOCPP.md#choosing-a-backend)). Vulkan is not yet confirmed on the verified models; reports welcome. | | Apple silicon | Metal. Installers exist; none of the verified models has been confirmed on a Mac yet. | | No dedicated GPU | Works, slowly. A clip that takes seconds on a GPU takes minutes on the CPU. | Docker and running from source (Linux arm64 included) are under [Run from source](#run-from-source). ### Install with a prompt Paste this into Claude Code, Cursor or Codex: ```text Install Mirli on this machine and confirm it works, following https://github.com/HamSanders/soundbox/blob/main/docs/INSTALL-AGENT.md ``` The guide tells the agent to check the GPU and VRAM first, to show you each model's size and licence before downloading it, never to accept a non-commercial licence for you, and to finish by generating one sound and telling you where the WAV is. ## Hear it Each clip was generated by Mirli from the prompt shown. The [samples site](https://mirli.app/sfx/) has around 600 more. | | Prompt | Model | | |---|---|---|---| | Glass | *large window pane breaking, cracking then collapsing inward with long shards falling and shattering on a wooden floor* | Stable Audio 3.0 SFX | [▶ Listen](https://mirli.app/sfx/glass/glass-window-pane-break) | | Ambience | *heavy thunderstorm, driving rain with rolling thunder and wind gusting through trees, outdoor, seamless loop* | Stable Audio 3.0 SFX | [▶ Listen](https://mirli.app/sfx/rain/rain-thunderstorm-full) | | Game | *plasma bolt firing, thick electric discharge with a downward pitch sweep and a crackling tail* | Stable Audio 3.0 SFX | [▶ Listen](https://mirli.app/sfx/laser/laser-plasma-bolt) | | Instrumental | *1980s synthwave arcade title theme, wide analog saw lead, gated reverb drum machine, pulsing sidechained bass, 110 BPM* | Stable Audio 3.0 Small Music | [▶ Listen](https://mirli.app/music/neon-arcade-nights) | | Song | *triumphant power pop victory anthem, bright electric guitars, punchy live drums, gang vocal chorus*, with a four-line lyric sheet | ACE-Step 1.5 | [▶ Listen](https://mirli.app/music/victory-lap) | ## For agents Start Mirli, then add it to your client. ```bash claude mcp add --transport http soundbox http://127.0.0.1:17494/mcp ``` Cursor and other MCP clients take `{ "type": "http", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:17494/mcp" }`. Then ask: "add a door slam and a coin pickup to this game", "voice these three lines as two characters", "write a 20-second loading-screen loop". The agent gets 24 tools for sounds, speech and multi-track stories, and three skills: `soundbox-sfx`, `soundbox-sound-pass` and `soundbox-voice-story`. Every tool, the stdio bridge and the skills are in [docs/MCP.md](docs/MCP.md). ## Models Every model runs through [audio.cpp](docs/AUDIOCPP.md), a native runtime, so there is no Python to set up. Verified end to end and on by default: | Model | Good for | Licence | Commercial use | |---|---|---|---| | **Stable Audio 3.0 SFX** | Sound effects, foley, ambience | Stability AI Community | ⚠️ Under $1M revenue | | **Stable Audio 3.0 Small Music** | Instrumental music, loops | Stability AI Community | ⚠️ Under $1M revenue | | **ACE-Step 1.5 Turbo** | Songs with lyrics; extend, cover, repaint | MIT | ✅ Yes | | **MiniMax Music 3** | Songs with lyrics, about 10 GB VRAM | MiniMax-Music3 Community | ⚠️ Conditional |
61 more in the catalog · 45 text-to-speech, 6 music, 2 SFX, 4 stem separation, 4 voice conversion
| Kind | Count | Includes | |---|---|---| | Text-to-speech | 45 | Chatterbox, Fish Audio S2 Pro, IndexTTS 2, VibeVoice, Higgs Audio v3, Qwen3-TTS, CosyVoice 3, Kokoro and more; several clone from a reference clip | | Music | 6 | ACE-Step 1.5 Base and XL, Stable Audio 3.0 Medium, HeartMuLa, MiniMax H3 | | Sound effects | 2 | MiDashengLM-Gen, ControlFoley | | Stem separation | 4 | HTDemucs (4- and 6-stem), BS-RoFormer, Mel-Band RoFormer | | Voice conversion | 4 | RVC, Seed-VC, MioCodec, MeanVC2 | VibeVoice 1.5B, MiDashengLM-Gen, HTDemucs 6-stem and Chatterbox Turbo have also been run end to end; the rest are marked unverified until someone reports. The 19 added in October 2026 need audio.cpp 0.9.2 or newer (`soundbox model install audiocpp` fetches the latest).
Any model whose licence could not be established is treated as non-commercial. This is a summary, not legal advice: read each licence before you ship what a model made. ## Compared with a hosted service | | Hosted (ElevenLabs, Suno and similar) | Mirli | |---|---|---| | Runs on | Their GPUs | Your machine | | Cost | Subscription or credits | Your electricity | | Account | Required | None | | Models | Closed, tuned, consistent | Open weights; quality varies by model | | Output rights | Their terms of service | The licence of the model that made it, shown up front | | Offline | No | Yes, once the weights are downloaded | | Agents | HTTP API | HTTP API and an MCP server | | Source | Closed | MIT | ## Run from source
Node, Docker and the HTTP API
Requires Node 22.12 or later. No Python, no CUDA toolkit. ```bash git clone https://github.com/HamSanders/soundbox cd soundbox npm install npm run dev ``` This starts the server on port 17494 and the UI on . `npm run dev:mock` runs the UI with no GPU or server (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)). **Docker.** The server and web UI run headless in one container with the audio.cpp runtime inside. CPU by default; add the CUDA override for a GPU. Both pull the prebuilt image from GHCR (`:latest`, `:cuda`, or a version such as `:v0.4.0` and `:v0.4.0-cuda`). ```bash docker compose up -d docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.cuda.yml up -d ``` To build from the checkout instead, add `-f docker-compose.build.yml` (and `-f docker-compose.build-cuda.yml` for CUDA) and `--build`; see [docs/INSTALL.md](docs/INSTALL.md#docker). details.readme:
raea

Render Anything Engine (for Anyone)

Tell your AI what to make. Videos, motion graphics, 3D and games, written as React and TypeScript
(the code your AI already writes) and rendered on your own GPU, faster than they play.

raea.io · Made in raea · Why raea · Docs · Releases

--- > **0.1.6** (17 November 2026) is the latest release: the engine and the desktop app on macOS (Apple Silicon), Linux > (x86_64) and, newest and least tested, Windows 10 and 11 (x86_64). raea is young and moves fast, with a release most > days since 0.1.1 on 11 November: expect rough edges, and tell us what you hit in an > [issue](https://github.com/shinyobjectz/raea/issues), or from your agent with `raea bug`. ## The app The raea app is where you make video, 3D and games with your AI. You ask in a chat; your own AI (Claude, ChatGPT, Kimi or a local model) writes the raea code and renders it; what it makes lands in the project's feed, where you watch it, scrub it, mark it up and send it back with notes. Download it from [raea.io](https://raea.io) for the Mac, Windows or Linux. It tells you when a new version is out; on the Mac it updates itself.

New to the app? **[Watch the tutorial](https://media.raea.io/#goose-learns-raea)** (5:50). What the app does now: - **The chat comes first** (0.1.5): your projects in a rail, the conversation in the middle, and `/goal` to keep an agent going until a condition you set holds. - **A timeline you edit by hand** (0.1.4): trim, split and move clips, speed curves, freeze frames and keys, the way CapCut works, under every film, sound and scene. - **Scenes you walk around in** (0.1.3): your agent posts a 3D scene and you walk through it, pin comments in it and move its parts by hand; every change is written into the scene's own code. - **Index** (0.1.5): your folders, drives and Apple Photos made searchable by what's in them, on your Mac. On an M5 Pro, 10,000 pictures were searchable in under a minute. - **Review** (0.1.6): each project has a Review tab, every comment you leave reaches the agent, and export is one window. - **Lighter** (0.1.6): the window gives back memory it's finished with and rests when nothing changes, 34% less CPU at rest. The app and the engine are free. Pro adds cloud storage, search across your computers and publishing; Team puts up to five people on one plan ([pricing](https://raea.io/pricing/)). Each release's notes are on the [releases page](https://github.com/shinyobjectz/raea/releases). ## Install ```sh curl -fsSL https://raea.io/install | sh ``` The installer puts the `raea` command under `~/.raea`, links it into `~/.local/bin`, and adds raea's agent skills to `~/.claude/skills`, so Claude Code (or any agent that reads that folder) knows how to write, render and check raea work. Run it again to update. The engine is free and needs no account. Tarballs and checksums are on the [releases page](https://github.com/shinyobjectz/raea/releases). On Windows 10 or 11, in PowerShell: ```powershell irm https://raea.io/install.ps1 | iex ``` It does the same under `~\.raea` and adds raea to your PATH. raea needs a DirectX 12 or Vulkan GPU driver; what else it needs (the Visual C++ runtime, FFmpeg and uv) is in its `bin\` folder. ## Hello A composition is a React component that draws a frame for a given moment: ```tsx import { AbsoluteFill, Composition, interpolate, registerRoot, useCurrentFrame } from "raea"; function Hello() { const f = useCurrentFrame(); return Hello; } registerRoot(() => ); ``` ```sh raea render hello.tsx -o hello.mp4 ``` On an Apple Silicon Mac those 90 frames render in about a second. The same file can play live as a game (`raea play`), render one frame for an agent to look at (`-o frame.png --frame 45`), or be checked against a quality floor (`raea check hello.mp4`). `raea init` starts a project, and `raea --help` lists every verb. ## What it does - **Video and motion graphics.** Layout, text, Tailwind, SVG and animation, composited on the GPU and encoded in hardware where the machine has it. Footage is cut by what's said in it (`raea cut`), and `raea check` catches clipped text, low contrast, unsafe areas, freezes and loudness problems before anyone watches. - **Games.** Input, physics, sound and 3D, played live with `raea play`, and exported as a program of their own (`raea export-game`). - **3D.** Scenes in TypeScript drawn by [Bevy](https://bevyengine.org) 0.20: cameras, lights, materials, glTF models, Gaussian splats, and Bevy plugins compiled into the engine. three.js work runs as it's written: a React Three Fiber scene inside ``, or a three.js page's script inside ``. - **Sound.** One mixer for live play and offline render, instruments and effects, and local models for foley and instrument notes (`raea sao`, `raea tokensynth`). - **Built for agents.** Everything it draws stays queryable as data, so an agent can render a frame, look at it, and fix what's wrong without a person in the loop. ## Made in raea Films, music videos, a tutorial and a game made with raea are on [media.raea.io](https://media.raea.io). Six of them come with their source in [raea-films](https://github.com/shinyobjectz/raea-films): each project's code under Apache-2.0, to read, render and take apart, and its models, textures and sound for anyone with a free raea account. ## Use it from your agent - **Agent skills.** They live in [raea-skills](https://github.com/shinyobjectz/raea-skills), pinned here as [`skills/`](skills): `raea` teaches an agent to write, render and check raea compositions, 3D and games included. The installer adds it to `~/.claude/skills`, and `raea skills install --agent NAME` to other agents. - **Claude plugin.** The raea skill and two hooks (raea's quick check after a composition is saved, and media shown in the raea app). In Claude Code: `/plugin install raea --marketplace shinyobjectz/raea-skills`. It's the `skills/` folder of raea-skills, and `/plugin marketplace add shinyobjectz/raea` installs the same one. - **Craft guides.** `raea guide` prints the floor every edit is held to and the guides for pitches, explainers, stories, games, motion, music and layout. `raea context PROJECT` says what to read before working on a project. - **Bug reports.** When an agent finds a bug in raea itself, `raea bug TITLE --text TEXT` sends it to raea's server with raea's version and the OS, no account needed. It sends words only: paths, emails and keys are taken out before it goes, and `--dry-run` prints what would go. ## Build from source Requirements: [Rust](https://rustup.rs) (rustup reads the pinned version from rust-toolchain.toml), [bun](https://bun.sh) and CMake. On macOS, Xcode's command-line tools; on Linux, the ALSA, fontconfig, udev, xkbcommon (with its X11 part, which the app targets' windows also load at run time) and Vulkan libraries and NASM (Ubuntu: `cmake ninja-build nasm libasound2-dev libfontconfig1-dev libudev-dev libvulkan-dev libxkbcommon-dev libxkbcommon-x11-dev`), as public CI installs them. ```sh git clone https://github.com/shinyobjectz/raea && cd raea cargo build --release -p raea-cli --no-default-features for d in sdk/raea sdk/react/js sdk/react/tw; do (cd $d && bun install); done target/release/raea render sdk/react/bench/games/pong/edit.tsx -o pong.mp4 ``` `--no-default-features` builds the public engine, as the releases are. The default features add one hosted service, Content Credentials signed by raea's signing server, which isn't part of this repository. raea sends nothing on its own: no telemetry, crash reports or update checks. What reaches the network is what you ask for (a remote URL in a composition, a model downloaded on first use, a `raea gen` step on a provider you hold a key for), and `RAEA_OFFLINE=1` refuses all of it. [docs/settings.md](docs/settings.md) lists the settings raea reads. ## What's in here The workspace is layered, from pure building blocks up to the command. | Folder | What | |---|---| | [`core/`](core) | Pure building blocks: the kernel language (K, interpreted on the CPU and compiled to WGSL), easing and animation, shapes, fonts, the scene and wire formats | | [`gpu/`](gpu) | The one shared GPU device and its telemetry | | [`io/`](io) | Decode and encode (VideoToolbox, software codecs, AV1, a muxer), files, network, npm packages, traces | | [`systems/`](systems) | Engine systems: layout, canvas, compositing, filters, mixing, speech, ML on ONNX Runtime, footage reading, lighting, contact checks for 3D parts, splats | | [`runtime/`](runtime) | Running a composition: the JavaScript engine seam (JavaScriptCore on macOS, QuickJS elsewhere), React and HTML on Bevy, baking, encode, live play | | [`engine/`](engine) | The renderer (`engine/render`), the in-process TypeScript bundler, the Bevy plugin catalog, and the `raea` command itself (`engine/cli`) | | [`apps/`](apps) | The crates behind the CLI's verbs: check, play, games, media | | [`sdk/`](sdk) | `raea`, the TypeScript SDK (`sdk/raea`), its 3D, physics, audio, video and UI packages, the craft guides, and the agent skills | | [`vendor/`](vendor) | Patched upstream crates, under their own licences ([`vendor/vendor.toml`](vendor/vendor.toml) says why each is patched) | | [`tools/`](tools) | Build and release helpers | Behaviour specs written in Gherkin (`.feature`) sit beside the code they describe. ## Licence raea is under the [Functional Source License 1.1, ALv2 Future License](LICENSE) (FSL-1.1-ALv2), copyright Shane Murphy. Use it, change it, build on it and pass it on for anything except a product that competes with raea. Each version becomes Apache-2.0 two years after its release. Third-party parts keep their own licences; see [NOTICE](NOTICE).

# Awesome Jev [![Awesome](https://awesome.re/badge.svg)](https://awesome.re)

> Discover Jev-powered apps, developer resources, and runnable decision examples.

[Jev](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction) is TypeSafe AI's System One model: give it state and typed questions, then use the returned choices, scores, and probabilities in your code. This independent community directory collects applications that use Jev, resources for developers, and small, inspectable workflows to learn from.

**[Explore Jev-powered apps](community/projects/apps/README.md)** · **[Share your app](CONTRIBUTING.md#list-a-jev-powered-app)**

**Try the beta web UI at [JevList](https://jevlist.ai/).** Explore the projects in this directory through a searchable web interface. We're continually improving the experience—take a look and let us know what you think!

## Contents

- [Explore Jev with our skill](#explore-jev-with-our-skill)
- [Start here](#start-here)
  - [Explore practical use cases](docs/explore-use-cases.md)
- [Official SDKs and tools](#official-sdks-and-tools)
- [Community projects](#community-projects)
  - [Community knowledge base](community/knowledge-base/README.md)
  - [Apps powered by Jev](#apps-powered-by-jev)
  - [Browse the project directory](community/projects/README.md)
  - [Tools and integrations](community/projects/tools/README.md)
- [Computer and browser use](#computer-and-browser-use)
- [Starter projects](#starter-projects)
- [Reference project](#reference-project)
- [Patterns and cookbooks](#patterns-and-cookbooks)
  - [Routing and classification](#routing-and-classification)
  - [Retrieval and verification](#retrieval-and-verification)
  - [Extraction and structured data](#extraction-and-structured-data)
- [Model behavior and evaluation](#model-behavior-and-evaluation)
- [Contributing](#contributing)

## Explore Jev with our skill

Use **Awesome Jev Guide** to understand Jev and explore solutions that fit your needs. Describe your workflow in plain language, and your coding agent will help you choose an example, adapt a project, or build a suitable starter—with guided setup along the way.

**1. Install the skill.** With Node.js 22+ installed, run this in your project directory:

```sh
npx skills add AppitStudio/awesome-jev --skill awesome-jev-guide
```

Select your coding agent when prompted. For Codex, you can add `--agent codex`. No TypeSafe account or API key is needed to explore ideas or run the offline examples.

**2. Open your coding agent in that project and try a prompt.**

New to Jev? Start here:

```text
Use awesome-jev-guide. Explain Jev simply, help me understand what I can
build with it, and walk me through the easiest example. I don't have
an API key yet.
```

Have a workflow in mind? Fill in the brackets:

```text
Use awesome-jev-guide. Today I [describe the work I do manually].
I want to [describe the result]. I use [language, framework, or tools].
Help me find the best starting point in this repo and explain what
needs adapting. Ask me anything essential that's missing.
```

Ready to build?

```text
Use awesome-jev-guide to build a small starter for [my workflow] using
[my stack]. Start with a working offline demo, explain what I should
customize, then guide me through API-key setup and a first live check
when I'm ready.
```

**3. Follow the next step together.** The guide uses current TypeSafe documentation and explains what already works, what needs building, and how to handle uncertain results. When you want live access, it walks you through private key setup—never paste a key into chat.

See the [full onboarding guide](docs/using-the-guide.md) for installation options, demos, and setup details.

## Start here

**[Explore what you can build](docs/explore-use-cases.md)** — choose a real implementation by the result you want, then follow its guide, worked example, and setup path.

- [Introduction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction) - Understand Jev's state-and-questions interface and its three decision primitives.
- [Official quick start](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/quickstart) - Make a first request using Python or HTTP.
- [Run an example locally](docs/getting-started.md) - Try a complete workflow with synthetic mock responses, without an account, an API key, or package installation.
- [Choose a decision pattern](docs/decision-patterns.md) - Match a task to Choice, Score, or Noul and define what happens when the result is uncertain.
- [HTTP API reference](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api) - Check the wire format, authentication, answer fields, and error responses.

## Official SDKs and tools

These resources are maintained by TypeSafe.

- [Agent skill](https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill) - Official docs for giving a coding agent API context and guidance when designing narrow System One / Jev decision questions (Claude Code plugin and skills.sh install paths).
- [JavaScript SDK](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-js) - JavaScript and TypeScript client that infers answer types from the supplied questions.
- [Python SDK](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-python) - Synchronous and asynchronous clients with typed answers and configurable retries.
- [System One Adapter](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/system-one-adapter-python) - Run a similar typed-question interface against other LLM providers for comparisons; those responses do not come from Jev.
- [TypeSafe Agent Skills](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/skills) - Official Claude Code / skills.sh agent skill for designing typed System One / Jev decisions; [docs](https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill).

## Community projects

The [community knowledge base](community/knowledge-base/README.md) turns credited articles into original implementation guides with source links, project connections and stated validation limits.

# World Walker

**v1.18.0** · English · [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md) · [Architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md) · [MCP mode](docs/MCP_PLAY.md) · [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md)

World Walker is a single-player AI tabletop RPG engine. You talk to the GM in plain language; a deterministic rules engine owns checks, prices, inventory, relationships, saves and replay. Any OpenAI-compatible `/chat/completions` endpoint can drive the story.

No host app. No provider lock-in. The model writes the scene; the engine owns the truth.

`217 rule functions` · `73 MCP tools` · `28 player tools` · `6 setting bundles` · `9 templates` · `24 self-check suites` · `0 runtime dependencies`

## Why it exists

Most AI RPGs fail in the same places. World Walker puts the boundaries in the engine, not in a longer prompt.

- **The GM cannot play your character.** It describes the world and NPCs; your decisions stay yours.
- **NPCs only know what they have seen.** A character cannot quote facts outside their witnessed memory.
- **A turn must leave a trace.** Every reply carries a scene card and an audit; a turn without a visible consequence is flagged.

A campaign is built at the table, not pre-written. Session Zero asks genre, play style, role, tone, difficulty and boundaries. Then each turn runs `scene card → your action → world reaction → state change → next hook`.

## Install and play

```bash
pip install -e ".[mcp]"      # core uses only the standard library; mcp is optional
wg init my-game.json
wg play --state my-game.json
```

`wg play` opens the local page at `http://127.0.0.1:8899/`. Continue a save or start a new world. The player view is one screen: narrative on the left, a narrow character and quest rail on the right, one input at the bottom.

`wg` is the entry point: `init`, `setup`, `play`, `serve`, `mcp`, `run`, `doctor`, `version`. `wg --help` lists the rest.

`wg setup` writes the five built-in narrative skill packs, a director note and two table rules to `~/.world-walker/harness.json` with `0600` permissions. An existing config is kept; use `--force` to rewrite it.

## Knowledge library

The lobby's “Start from a prefab or archive” entry offers six selectable starts: island survival, Nine Wastes, Fog Port, Neon Abyss, Sword Break, and the Xuan Gate. A prefab fixes the world, play loop, difficulty, tone and narrative style; name, role, boundaries and what happens next still belong to the player.

“Design archives” holds the raft, prefab-authoring and release-discipline notes. The data lives in `library/playbooks/*.json` and `library/archives/*.md` and ships with the package.

## Use your own model

The model layer only assumes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint:

```json
{ "base_url": "https://your-gateway/v1", "api_key": "sk-...", "model": "any-model" }
```

Set it in the model settings page, or use `WW_MODEL_BASE_URL`, `WW_MODEL_API_KEY` and `WW_MODEL_NAME`. The config lives at `~/.world-walker/model.json` with `0600` permissions.

## Tune the GM

The “Connect & tune → Narrative tuning” panel keeps four layers separate instead of folding taste, prompt packs and hard rules into one switch:

- **Prompt:** director notes and table rules are appended to the GM system prompt. They change the telling, not POLICY, CANON or numeric outcomes.
- **Narrative skills:** prompt packs under `narrative_skills/*.md`, each with a title and summary, injected only when enabled. These are not character skills.
- **Engine rules:** the current save's `rulebook`, ordered by `order`, limited to whitelisted effects. Validate and save from the panel; trigger counts are persisted. Rules can run at turn start or after every tool result.
- **Turn hooks:** `before_turn.py`, `after_tool.py` and `after_turn.py` under `~/.world-walker/hooks`. Off by default. They run with your own permissions — treat them as Python you wrote yourself.

Tuning config lives at `~/.world-walker/harness.json` with `0600` permissions. Prompts, skills, hooks and rules for an external agent still belong to its host; World Walker only supplies MCP tools and starting prompts.

## Connect an agent over MCP

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "world-walker": { "command": "world-walker-mcp" } } }
```

Any MCP client works. For remote agents, use HTTP instead of stdio:

```bash
wg mcp --http --port 8620
```

Then point the client at `http://127.0.0.1:8620/mcp`. A complete game can start with one setting bundle and one trade:

```
load_setting(path="settings/玄枢界.setting.json")
trade(location="临川城", item="ningyuan_dan", direction="buy", quantity=1)
```

The host calls tools only when a number is needed. Prose stays in the conversation.

## What the engine owns

- **Checks and combat:** d20, 2d6, d100, 4dF, dice pools, opposed rolls, damage and death rules.
- **Economy and people:** prices, inventory, relationships, reputation, debts and faction shifts.
- **World movement:** clocks, rumors, roaming NPCs, clues, quest stages and long-run consequences.
- **Replay:** one transactional writer, a command log with state fingerprints, and a save you can inspect.
- **Context boundaries:** NPC knowledge, canon facts, world book triggers and a scene card before every reply.

The player surface exposes 28 tools. The 73-tool MCP surface remains for advanced hosts. Both routes share the same rules, state file and writer.

## Quality

Verification is executable, not decorative. `scripts/verify_*.py`, behaviour regressions and mutation tests must fail when the code is wrong. The main gate runs 24 self-check suites, with coverage for the core domain and a zero-survivor mutation pass.

```bash
python3 scripts/verify_docs.py
python3 scripts/verify_player_shell.py
python3 scripts/verify_mcp_stdio.py
```

## Saves and failure

Saves use atomic replacement with a `.bak` fallback and a re-entrant Windows/POSIX lock. Crash tests cover several interruption windows.

If `<state>.archive-pending` or `.ww-session-transaction-pending` exists, protected reads and writes are refused. There is **no automatic recovery**: stop writing, preserve the evidence and review it manually. Restoring the caller's in-memory state after a failed save is **not an archive rollback**. See [the archive recovery guide](docs/ARCHIVE_RECOVERY.md).

## Scope

Built for single-player AI GM play, setting bundles, local saves and MCP hosts. Deliberately not multiplayer, cloud accounts, a plugin marketplace or pre-written campaigns sold as content.

## Project layout

```
world-walker/                  # repo root is the game_engine package
├── panel.py                   # player HTTP/SSE server and game APIs
├── dialog_runtime.py          # GM prompt, tool loop, turn finish and audit
├── narrative_rules.py         # Session Zero, scene cards, turn audit
├── rules/                     # deterministic settlement
├── settings/                  # six ready-to-play worlds
├── saves/                     # local save library
└── scripts/                   # verification and build tools
```

## License

MIT. Demo names, factions and places are original; no setting material from existing works is reused.
